entities.name: Temple of Earth
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Temple of Earth (Dìtán, 地坛) in Beijing, also known as the Square Altar of Earth (Fangze Tan), is one of the four major royal sacrifice altars of imperial Beijing — complementing the Temple of Heaven (for sacrifices to Heaven), the Temple of the Sun (for solar sacrifices), and the Temple of the Moon (for lunar sacrifices) — and was the site where the Emperor of China offered annual sacrifices to the Earth God at the Summer Solstice, embodying the cosmological framework of imperial Chinese governance in which the emperor served as the intermediary between Heaven and Earth.

Ditan was constructed in 1530 during the Jiajing Emperor's reign in the Ming Dynasty, as part of a systematic restructuring of Beijing's sacrificial altar network. The altar is square (representing Earth in Chinese cosmology, contrasting with Heaven's circular form) and situated to the north of the Imperial City, as the traditional cosmological association placed Earth in the north (Yin direction). The Jiajing Emperor, who also established the Temple of Heaven in its current form, comprehensively reorganized China's state sacrificial system according to classical ritual texts.

The Summer Solstice ceremony at Ditan was one of the most important state rituals in the Chinese imperial calendar — the Emperor would arrive in formal procession, perform ablutions and fasting, and offer ritual sacrifices to ensure the Earth's continued fertility and the stability of the agricultural foundation of Chinese civilization. Today Ditan Park is a public space in central Beijing and hosts Spring Festival fairs that attract millions of visitors annually, representing the conversion of imperial ritual space into popular public culture.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Temple of Earth (Ditan) — completing Beijing's imperial cosmological sacrifice system, embodying Chinese imperial governance's intermediary role between Heaven and Earth, and now a beloved public park — is a significant monument of Ming Dynasty ritual organization and Chinese cosmological worldview.
